Description

Timeseries related functions require access to the timestamp field (typically @timestamp). Currently, the functions declare a UnresolvedAttribute(@timestamp) inside their constructor:
 

so that the Analyzer injects it however this has several disadvantages:
- it hardcodes the field name which makes the resolution fail in case of a rename for example ts indices- | rename x = @timestamp | ...
- if the public constructor is called after the analysis phase, the plan becomes invalid

An improved approach is to be explicit about the dependency and instruct the planner to deal with across the entire query in a holistic fashion.
One approach is to introduce a dedicated TimestampAwareBuilder (similar to ConfigurationAware ) to handle the constructor reference or simply rely on the TimestampAware interface to mark the consumer and (potentially a (a TimestampSource for the provider to clearly indicate the @timestamp either through a dedicated method or through its type/"flag" similar to MetadataAttribute but not by name since it's an actual user facing field).

 
In the function registry define

 
An alternative to TimestampAwareBuilder is to check if the target function implements TimestampAware interface and if so, look at the constructor field of time Expression based on the @Param annotation information. The former should be more reliable since it applies to all constructors whereas @Param is used for documentation purposes.

The advantage of this approach is the resolution and supplying of the timestamp is externalized from the function into the registry which can wire the field directly similar to the approach taken with Configuration.
It's up to the instantiators of the function to supply the timestamp instead of the function itself, the current situation.
kept_issues.title: ESQL: Introduce TimestampAware interface/contract

Most of this issue description is just an explanation of the nature of the status quo. At the end I'll propose some possible future enhancements that might help improve things.

Consider these examples:

 

There's a set processor with an if: condition, and (abstractly) that if: condition is there to check if some value is within some set. As written, I think the code is exceedingly clear. Unfortunately, the runtime effect of this is not especially performant.

To my understanding, when painless encounters a constant expression list construction, like ['a', 'b', 'c'] it allocates a new ArrayList with the default capacity (10), and then adds the things that it finds one at a time. If the default capacity isn't big enough, then the ArrayList will automatically resize itself (growing by half each time, and copying all the existing members; so it goes 10->15->22, etc). So that's all kinda not great -- it means we're O(N) in time and space on the constants in the literal list part of the .contains(...) (with an unfortunately high lost constant term on the O(N)). Beyond that, the .contains check itself is a linear scan though the list checking for equality as it goes, so that's another O(N) term.

It's not super obvious how somebody could do better in terms of writing painless scripts, but I've investigated a few options:

1. For small sets, it's reasonable to unroll into ctx.foo == 'a' || ctx.foo == 'b' || ctx.foo == 'c' || .... This is quite fast, but still fundamentally a linear scan. It is allocation free.

2. For the criminally devious, a regex avoids most of the collections overhead, and is actually the fastest option I benchmarked (not by much, but it's worth mentioning). That could look like this: /(?:alfa|bravo|charlie|delta|echo|foxtrot|golf|hotel|india|juliett|kilo)/.matcher(ctx.message).matches(). That allocates a new Matcher object on each invocation, so it's not allocation free, but in the best case it could return false after a single character comparison, so that's pretty nifty. I do not think it wins any points for readability.

3. Only slightly slower than the regex, though, is a static params map that allows access to a containsKey check, like this (note: I award myself a gold star for abusing map keys to get actual set semantics and performance):

 

4. Finally, a simpler version of the same trick still has a single static params list and a linear scan, but avoids the annoying overhead of the list construction per invocation (and the annoying synax of either a regex or a too-clever-by-half map):

 

This last version is still allocation free, and it turns out that a linear scan through, say, a 20 element list isn't actually all that much slower in practice than a map lookup (of course it won't keep scaling too well as N gets bigger, but for small values of N the difference between an O(N) scan and a O(1) lookup that has to hashCode the String that it's looking up isn't all that enormous, at least on this developer's machine).

For my money, I think this last approach wins, then, in terms of performance and readability.

-----

I have three thoughts on what might be done about this:

1. It might be very clever to presize the ArrayList capacity for a constant expression, rather than allocating an ArrayList with the default size.

2. It might be nice to have some kind of static/const keyword so that a constant collection like this could be hoisted up in the code to make it clear that the collection is being created just once (in the code and at runtime).

3. Perhaps most cleverly, since the runtime performance of a linear scan isn't all that bad, a sufficiently advanced compiler could just emit a static ArrayList when it sees a .contains(...) check on a literal list of constants like the above examples.

Of all of these, I'm most enamored with option 3, but that's just me.

```
    }
```

This last version is still allocation free, and it turns out that a linear scan through, say, a 20 element list isn't actually all that much slower in practice than a map lookup (of course it won't keep scaling too well as N gets bigger, but for small values of N the difference between an O(N) scan and a O(1) lookup that has to `hashCode` the String that it's looking up isn't all that enormous, at least on this developer's machine).

For my money, I think this last approach wins, then, in terms of performance and readability.

-----

I have three thoughts on what might be done about this:

1. It might be very clever to presize the ArrayList capacity for a constant expression, rather than allocating an ArrayList with the default size.

2. It might be nice to have some kind of `static`/`const` keyword so that a constant collection like this could be hoisted up in the code to make it clear that the collection is being created just once (in the code and at runtime).

3. Perhaps most cleverly, since the runtime performance of a linear scan isn't all that bad, a sufficiently advanced compiler could just emit a `static` `ArrayList` when it sees a `.contains(...)` check on a literal list of constants like the above examples.

Of all of these, I'm most enamored with option 3, but that's just me.

-----

This is a very popular pattern for scripts, so I think it would be worth optimizing:

```
joegallo@simulacron:~/Code/elastic/integrations $ git grep '''].contains(' | grep 'if:' | wc -l
    1281
joegallo@simulacron:~/Code/elastic/integrations $ git grep '"].contains(' | grep 'if:' | wc -l
     245
```

Ideally, my preference would be that Elasticsearch/Painless just makes the existing code magically be faster (for example by pursuing option 3 above), but in the absence of that, it may be worthwhile to rewrite individual conditional statements (like to use a constant list in the params) for especially high volume integrations where throughput matters.

The minimum transport version of all clusters involved in the execution of a query is available to the coordinator's analyzer, optimizers and mapper. However, it is not available to the data node at all.

Let's send the minimum transport version to the data node and make it available to the optimizer contexts and the local mapper.

This is important for changes to aggregations that affect what data we send to the coordinator: All data nodes need to agree on the columns sent. Similarly to our existing optimizer tests, the fact that the local optimizers and planning will become version-aware needs a small update to our tests as well: we should generally assume a random version unless the test is specifically for a new way of optimizing/planning something, in which case we should assume a random version not lower than the new transport version required for this planning change.

### Description

Match query works with semantic_text fields in the query DSL and it applies prefiltering to other bool queries used with it (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/132068).

When using `MATCH` on semantic_text fields on ES|QL, it is possible that other filters are not pushable to Lucene. This means that they won't be included in the bool query that will be issued to Lucene, and thus won't be applied as pre-filters.

The way around this for the `KNN` function was to change the KNN query into an exact query, and apply the non-pushable filters as post-filters (see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/132944). Having KNN as an exact search function means we will find as much results as needed and the non-pushable filters will be applied, but as much results as possible will be retrieved back.

We can apply the same mechanism to `MATCH` when using a semantic_text field to ensure filtering is consistent when filters can't be pushed down.
kept_issues.title: ES|QL - MATCH function with semantic_text fields with non pushable filters

The ask

We would like a way to signal to Elasticsearch not to return partial results before an async search is completed, so that we can efficiently use the GET /_async_search/{id} endpoint for long-polling.

 The why

After creating an async search, Kibana currently uses the async status endpoint /_async_search/status/{id} for polling. The reason is that if we use GET /_async_search/{id}, we will always receive partial results if they are available. - it requires us to make two requests to detect a finished search and then load results

In practical terms, this means that every panel on a dashboard is being unnecessarily slowed down.

This enhancement will allow results to be delivered to the client _as soon as they are ready_.

### Description

## Summary

Elasticsearch needs a simple way to configure JVM log paths (GC logs, error dumps) via environment variable, without the complexity of parsing configuration files. This would enable separation of read-only installation directories from read/write runtime directories.

## Background

Related issues:
- #39091 - Declined due to complexity of coordinating multiple log path configurations (path.logs, log4j2.properties, JVM options)
- #39090 - Declined due to concerns about general environment variable substitution causing unexpected issues

The Windows service already uses `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` for `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Apache Software Foundation\Procrun 2.0\Instance\Parameters\Log\Path`, but this variable is not available in `jvm.options`.

I don't know how `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` is stored or utilized in linux machines, so I accept that it adds further complexity and consideration.

## Current Problem

**jvm.options currently uses hardcoded relative paths:**
```
-XX:ErrorFile=logs/hs_err_pid%p.log
-Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=logs/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=32,filesize=64m
```

These resolve relative to the working directory, not to any configured log location. Users cannot externalize JVM logs without editing jvm.options at installation time.

## Proposal

Make `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` available for substitution in `jvm.options`:

```
-XX:ErrorFile=${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}/hs_err_pid%p.log
-Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=32,filesize=64m
```

**Implementation:** Startup scripts perform simple string replacement of `${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}` before passing options to JVM. Default to `logs` if unset, but having installed without `SERVICE_LOG_DIR`, I believe it already defaults to `<Installation Directory>\logs`.

### This Does NOT Require:
- Parsing elasticsearch.yml
- Parsing log4j2.properties
- Coordinating multiple log configurations
- General environment variable substitution (avoiding edge cases like `:` or `_` in keys, which, per example, causes IConfiguration to break in dotnet)
- Changes to Elasticsearch application logging

### This ONLY Provides:
- **One specific variable** (`SERVICE_LOG_DIR`) for **one specific purpose** (JVM-level logs)
- String substitution in startup scripts (same pattern as `ES_TMPDIR` on line 56)
- Consistency with existing Windows service configuration
- The opportunity to configure jvm.options with a subdirectory (`/jvm/`) to organize JVM logs separately from application logs

### This COULD Provide:
- A way to use the variable within the elasticsearch.yml, if you want.
- A way to use the variable in log4j2.properties, if you want.

## Use Cases

**1. Security Hardening**
```
C:\Program Files\Elasticsearch\        (read-only, executables only)
C:\ProgramData\Elasticsearch\data\     (read/write, data)
C:\ProgramData\Elasticsearch\logs\jvm\ (read/write, JVM logs)
```
Following principle of least privilege by preventing write access to installation directory.

**2. Unified Log Location**
All logs (application + JVM) in one place for backup, monitoring, or export:
```
/var/log/elasticsearch/           (application logs via path.logs)
/var/log/elasticsearch/jvm/       (JVM logs via SERVICE_LOG_DIR)
```
Single directory to mount/export/monitor. No need to search multiple locations.

**3. Windows Service Alignment**
Currently `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` controls procrun logs but not GC/error logs, creating inconsistent locations. This would unify them.

## Why This Avoids Previous Objections

- **Not an edge case:** Read-only installation directories are a standard security practice
- **No configuration complexity:** Only affects JVM logs, not the multiple application log configurations
- **Minimal scope:** One variable, not general substitution that could cause parsing issues
- **Follows existing pattern:** `ES_TMPDIR` already works this way (line 56 of jvm.options)

## Backward Compatibility

Default to `logs` if `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` not set, maintaining current behavior.

The MMR algorithm follows a simple but effective process:

1. Start by selecting the most relevant item
2. For each remaining item, calculate an MMR score that combines:
   - Its relevance to the query
   - Its dissimilarity to already selected items
3. Select the item with the highest MMR score
4. Repeat until you have enough results


The MMR score formula at step 2 is:

```
MMR(Di) = lambda * similarity(Q,Di)) - (1-lambda)(max(similarity(Di, Dj))
```

where:
- Di is the current doc we compute the MMR score
- Dj represent the docs from the diversified result set
- Q is the query vector (which can be optional)

Let's assume we have N docs that we need to diversify.
In our current implementation of MMR, we maintain two sets of caches:
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between the query Q and all documents (N size)
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between pairs of documents Di,Dj (N*N size)

At step, for each document that we have not selected we recompute the MMR score, using these two caches.

We can reduce the number of computations, the cache size and the number of cache lookups by maintaining:
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between the query Q and all documents (N size)
- a cache that holds max similarity between the current doc and the diversified set of docs (N size)

We no longer need a cache for all pairs of `similarity(Di, Dj)`.

Assume we have selected document `Dx` at step 2 and we are now looking at adding a new document to the diversified set.
The new MMR score becomes:

```
// update the cache for maxSimilarityToSelected 
maxSimilarityToSelected(Di) = max(similarity(Di, Dx), maxSimilarityToSelected(Di))

MMR(Di) = lambda * similarity(Q,Di)) - (1-lambda) * maxSimilarityToSelected(Di)
```

With this method we no longer have to iterate through all the already selected documents, when we compute a new MMR score.
We only need to take into account the last document we added to the list of diversified results.

When a shard relocation occurs, in-flight indexing operations wait to acquire a primary permit until the relocation completes. Upon successful relocation, these operations receive a RetryOnPrimaryException, which marks the request as retried. This forces a version lookup during indexing on the new primary, even for operations that could have used the auto-generated ID append-only optimization.

For shards with high indexing throughput, relocations can take a while to complete. During this time, many operations queue up, all marked as retried. When they finally execute on the new primary, they must perform version lookups (requiring at least a terms dictionary lookup) with a likely cold cache. This can overwhelm the new primary shard.

We should detect this situation and avoid marking the request as retried, since we can safely assume the documents were not indexed on the old primary.

Description

Issue: Group remaining values as “Other” when using LIMIT PER with time buckets
Summary

Users want to query top N values by a metric (e.g. client IPs by average bytes) over time, while also seeing an “Other” group that represents the aggregate of all remaining values per time bucket.

This pattern is common in visualizations such as histograms or time series charts, but it does not currently work as expected in ESQL when time-based bucketing is involved.

User problem

A typical use case is:

Identify the top 3 client IPs by a metric (e.g. average or percentile of bytes sent)

Show those top 3 IPs bucketed per hour

Also show an “Other” series, representing the aggregated metric of all remaining client IPs per hour

This is especially important for dashboards, where users want:

Focus on the most significant contributors

Still understand the behavior of the long tail over time

Example scenario

A user wants to:

Get the top 3 client IPs by average bytes sent

Visualize them in a histogram bucketed per hour

Include an “Other” bucket that shows the average bytes sent per hour by all remaining client IPs

This works in some simple cases, but fails when time intervals are introduced (e.g. 12-hour or 1-hour buckets).

Why this is a problem today

The current behavior makes it difficult or impossible to express this query pattern in ESQL because:

The query needs to:

Determine the top N values across the dataset

Then separately aggregate the remaining values (“Other”) using the same time buckets

Once the top N values are selected, the information needed to correctly compute the “Other” aggregation per time bucket is no longer available within the same query flow

As a result, users cannot reliably produce a single result set that includes:

Top N series per time bucket

Plus a correctly aggregated “Other” series per time bucket

Impact

Because of this limitation:

Common visualization patterns (Top N + Other over time) are hard to express

Tools like Kibana currently work around this by issuing multiple background queries

Users cannot easily reason about or reproduce the same logic directly in ESQL

Today (e.g. in 139124) we use TransportServicenewNetworkBytesStream to access the Netty allocator so that we can accumulate bytes for eventual network transmission, but also want to keep track of those bytes in a circuit breaker so that we can fail the accumulation process before it consumes too much heap. With the existing API the caller must accumulate some amount of memory and then update the circuit breaker to match, but it'd be preferable to adjust the circuit breaker before actually allocating the memory in the first place. The caller must also manually keep track of the bytes tracked in the circuit breaker so as to be sure to release them (as well as the actual pages) on all failure paths. The caller also has no practical way to account for the unused bytes in the last page.

I think instead we should offer a way to track the allocations in a circuit breaker as they occur, by adapting either RecyclerBytesStreamOutput or the underlying Recycler to do the necessary accounting directly.

### Motivation

ES|QL does not currently support a native way to paginate/scroll results.

There are ways to achieve this in ES|QL, but with additional effort.
Take for example the following query:

```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC, _id // _id here serves as a tiebreaker
| LIMIT 10
```

If we wanted to retrieve the next 10 documents, we could:
- reissue the same ES|QL query, but with `LIMIT 20` and then on the client side, skip the first 10 rows
- from the first 10 documents, take the values of `_score` and `_id` of the last row and add a filter:
```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC, _id
| LIMIT 20
| WHERE _score <= ?last_score AND _id > ?last_id
```

### Proposal

Introduce an OFFSET option to LIMIT

```
LIMIT x OFFSET y
```

Explanation: LIMIT will skip the first y rows and then keep x rows.

While OFFSET might not be the solution to all use cases that require pagination, it does cover many of them, the same way `from` and `size` cover most pagination use cases in `_search`.

### Execution

Take the following query:

```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC
| LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
```

The OFFSET will only be applied on the coordinator.
In order for this to work correctly, the data node plans will still need to return up to 10 + 20 sorted rows.

The OFFSET option will only be allowed if the input is sorted, e.g. if a SORT is used.
If we detect that OFFSET is used without SORT, we will return a verification error.
This means that OFFSET will only be applied by TopN.

Both Limit and TopN have their own unique optimizations in the planner, that will need to be given special consideration when OFFSET is introduced.


### Requirements/implementation checklist

- [ ] syntax change to introduce OFFSET to LIMIT (query params support for OFFSET)
- [ ] verification when OFFSET is used without SORT
- [ ] basic support (no optimization) for OFFSET with sorted input for basic queries e.g. `FROM index | SORT field | LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10`. 

Optimizations that need to correctly handle OFFSET:
- [ ] `CombineTopN`
- [ ] `HoistRemoteEnrichLimit`
- [ ] `HoistRemoteEnrichTopN`
- [ ] `PushDownAndCombineLimits`
- [ ] `PushDownFilterAndLimitIntoUnionAll`
- [ ] `ReplaceLimitAndSortAsTopN`
- [ ] `ReplaceTopNWithLimitAndSort`
- [ ] `PushDownLimitAndOrderByIntoFork`

- [ ] documentation

Summary

XContentParser.getTokenLocation() returns an XContentLocation(lineNumber, columnNumber). The underlying Jackson JsonParser provides byte offsets via JsonLocation.getByteOffset(), but JsonXContentParser discards this information when wrapping the Jackson location. Exposing byte offsets would enable zero-copy extraction of sub-structures (objects/arrays) from the source byte array.

 Motivation

The JSON_EXTRACT ES|QL function (142375) extracts values from JSON strings. When the extracted value is an object or array, it currently uses XContentBuilder.copyCurrentStructure(parser) to serialize the sub-structure back to JSON — walking every token and rebuilding the string from scratch, even though the original bytes are already valid JSON in the source array.

With byte offsets, extraction becomes a direct array slice:

 

This eliminates all intermediate parsing, string allocation, and JSON escaping for the sub-structure.

 Proposed API Change

XContentLocation — add byteOffset with a backward-compatible constructor:

 

XContentParser — add getCurrentLocation() (the other method already exists):

 

 Implementation Impact

The XContentParser hierarchy has 19 implementations. The change is concentrated in one place.

Leaf implementations (5):

| Class | Change needed | Notes |
|-------|--------------|-------|
| JsonXContentParser | Pass through JsonLocation.getByteOffset() instead of discarding it. Add getCurrentLocation() delegating to Jackson. | ~10 lines changed |
| SmileXContentParser | None — inherits from JsonXContentParser | |
| CborXContentParser | None — inherits from JsonXContentParser | |
| YamlXContentParser | None — inherits from JsonXContentParser. Jackson's YAML parser returns -1 for byte offsets (only char offsets available). | |
| MapXContentParser | Return -1 byte offset (no byte stream) | Trivial |

Decorators (13): All transparent — delegate through FilterXContentParser.delegate(). Zero changes needed for 11 of 13. The two with overrides:

| Class | Notes |
|-------|-------|
| DotExpandingXContentParser | Returns saved location for synthesized tokens — would carry -1 byte offset for synthetic tokens, real offsets for original content |
| CompletionFieldMapper.MultiFieldParser | Returns fixed location — would carry -1 byte offset |

Test-only (1): ParameterizableYamlXContentParser — delegates, transparent.

 Byte Slicing Feasibility by Format

Not all content types support raw byte slicing even with offsets available:

| Format | Byte offsets? | Slicing safe? | Why |
|--------|--------------|---------------|-----|
| JSON | Yes | Yes | Sliced sub-structure is valid standalone JSON |

## Summary

`XContentParser.getTokenLocation()` returns an `XContentLocation(lineNumber, columnNumber)`. The underlying Jackson `JsonParser` provides byte offsets via `JsonLocation.getByteOffset()`, but `JsonXContentParser` discards this information when wrapping the Jackson location. Exposing byte offsets would enable zero-copy extraction of sub-structures (objects/arrays) from the source byte array.

## Motivation

The `JSON_EXTRACT` ES|QL function (#142375) extracts values from JSON strings. When the extracted value is an object or array, it currently uses `XContentBuilder.copyCurrentStructure(parser)` to serialize the sub-structure back to JSON — walking every token and rebuilding the string from scratch, even though the original bytes are already valid JSON in the source array.

With byte offsets, extraction becomes a direct array slice:

```java
long start = parser.getTokenLocation().byteOffset();
parser.skipChildren();
long end = parser.getCurrentLocation().byteOffset();
builder.appendBytesRef(new BytesRef(bytes, offset + (int) start, (int) (end - start)));
```

This eliminates all intermediate parsing, string allocation, and JSON escaping for the sub-structure.

## Proposed API Change

**`XContentLocation`** — add `byteOffset` with a backward-compatible constructor:

```java
public record XContentLocation(int lineNumber, int columnNumber, long byteOffset) {
    public XContentLocation(int lineNumber, int columnNumber) {
        this(lineNumber, columnNumber, -1L);
    }
}
```

**`XContentParser`** — add `getCurrentLocation()` (the other method already exists):

```java
XContentLocation getTokenLocation();    // already exists — starts populating byteOffset
XContentLocation getCurrentLocation();  // new — position just past the last consumed byte
```

## Implementation Impact

The XContentParser hierarchy has 19 implementations. The change is concentrated in one place.

**Leaf implementations (5):**

| Class | Change needed | Notes |
|-------|--------------|-------|
| `JsonXContentParser` | Pass through `JsonLocation.getByteOffset()` instead of discarding it. Add `getCurrentLocation()` delegating to Jackson. | ~10 lines changed |
| `SmileXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser` | |
| `CborXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser` | |
| `YamlXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser`. Jackson's YAML parser returns `-1` for byte offsets (only char offsets available). | |
| `MapXContentParser` | Return `-1` byte offset (no byte stream) | Trivial |

**Decorators (13):** All transparent — delegate through `FilterXContentParser.delegate()`. Zero changes needed for 11 of 13. The two with overrides:

| Class | Notes |
|-------|-------|
| `DotExpandingXContentParser` | Returns saved location for synthesized tokens — would carry `-1` byte offset for synthetic tokens, real offsets for original content |
| `CompletionFieldMapper.MultiFieldParser` | Returns fixed location — would carry `-1` byte offset |

**Test-only (1):** `ParameterizableYamlXContentParser` — delegates, transparent.

## Byte Slicing Feasibility by Format

Not all content types support raw byte slicing even with offsets available:

| Format | Byte offsets? | Slicing safe? | Why |
|--------|--------------|---------------|-----|
| JSON | Yes | **Yes** | Sliced sub-structure is valid standalone JSON |
| CBOR | Yes | **Yes** | Self-contained data items, no back-references |
| SMILE | Yes | **No** | Back-references for repeated field names/strings — sliced fragment may contain unresolvable references |
| YAML | No (`-1`) | **No** | Whitespace-sensitive grammar, anchor/alias system |

Consumers must check the content type before slicing. JSON and CBOR are safe; SMILE and YAML require the `XContentBuilder.copyCurrentStructure` fallback.
kept_issues.title: Expose byte offsets on XContentParser for zero-copy sub-structure extraction

Currently, all merge-related settings in Elasticsearch — such as index.merge.scheduler.max_thread_count, index.merge.scheduler.max_merge_count, and index.merge.policy. — are scoped at the index/shard level. There is no node-level cap on the total number of concurrent merge threads.

I wonder if we can adding a node-level setting (e.g., node.merge.scheduler.max_thread_count) that caps the total concurrent merge threads across all shards on a node.

When we introduced `SET unmapped_fields="..."`, the default behavior was to fail every query that mentions unmapped fields (like ESQL behaved forever). So we called the default setting `fail`.

This is becoming a misnomer with https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/141532 changing the default behavior for `PROMQL` queries: we always nullify unmapped fields for such queries.

- [x] Let's fix this by renaming the default setting from `fail` to `default`; this leaves us more room for making standard ESQL queries behave in whichever way is best, and we can still add a `fail` option later that is _stricter_ than the default.
- [x] This is _technically_ breaking, but since `unmapped_fields` is in tech preview and the `fail` option has no effect on queries compared to just omitting `SET unmapped_fields="..."`, it's likely still fine to change. But we need to double check.
- [x] We need to also update the docs for the `unmapped_fields` SETting; should be easy, the docs are generated from the setting definition.
kept_issues.title: ESQL: rename unmapped_fields default setting from `fail` to `default`

This is the correct ECS interpretation ("when this event arrived in the data store") and the necessary time anchor for alerting deduplication.

### 1. Update results index mappings

**File**: `x-pack/plugin/core/template-resources/src/main/resources/ml/anomalydetection/results_index_mappings.json`

Add to the `"properties"` block:

```json
"event": {
  "properties": {
    "ingested": {
      "type": "date",
      "format": "strict_date_optional_time||epoch_millis"
    }
  }
}
```

Also increment `AnomalyDetectorsIndex.RESULTS_INDEX_MAPPINGS_VERSION` (`1` → `2`). This cascades to `MlIndexTemplateRegistry.ML_INDEX_TEMPLATE_VERSION`, triggering template reinstallation on cluster startup.

3. In `toXContent()`, write the stored value — **only if non-null** — as a nested object (not a dot-notation flat key):

```java
// Produces {"event": {"ingested": <epoch_millis>}}
if (eventIngested != null) {
    builder.startObject("event");
    builder.field("ingested", eventIngested.toEpochMilli());
    builder.endObject();
}
```

- `persistBucket(Bucket)` — set on `bucketWithoutRecords` (the copy used for indexing, not the original)
- `persistBucketInfluencersStandalone(...)` — set on each `BucketInfluencer` in the loop
- `persistInfluencers(List<Influencer>)` — set on each influencer in the loop

**Why not inside `toXContent()`?** `ScoresUpdater` + `JobRenormalizedResultsPersister` reads existing documents from the index as full Java objects, updates score fields, then re-serializes via `toXContent()` and re-indexes. - **Existing indices**: `ElasticsearchMappings.addDocMappingIfMissing()` is called in `OpenJobPersistentTasksExecutor` each time a job is opened. - **Existing documents**: Old documents do not gain the field retroactively. Kibana rules fall back to `timestamp`-range logic when `event.ingested` is absent (handled on the Kibana side).

## Problem

On a snapshot build, a query against a `date_range` field plans and executes successfully but fails when the response is requested in Arrow format:

```
ES|QL type [date_range] is not supported by the Arrow format
```

Source: [`ArrowResponse.java:52-54`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/arrow/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/arrow/ArrowResponse.java#L52-L54).

The `ESQL_CONVERTERS` map in `ArrowResponse.java:371` enumerates every ES|QL type that has an Arrow `BlockConverter`. `DATE_RANGE` was added as a `DataType` (marked `underConstruction(ESQL_LONG_RANGES)` in `DataType.java:310`) but no Arrow converter was registered alongside it.

## Broader gap

The Arrow converter registry is a flat `Map<String, BlockConverter>` keyed by type name. Nothing — neither build step, type system, nor test — catches "new `DataType` added without Arrow converter." A user only finds out at runtime, on an error that looks internal. This will recur every time a new type lands unless we close the loop.

## Suggested fix

Two parts:

### 1. Add a `date_range` Arrow converter.

Encoding options worth discussing:
- Fixed-size list of 2 `TIMESTAMPMILLI` (`[gte, lte]`).
- Struct with `gte` and `lte` fields.
- Arrow's `INTERVAL` / `DURATION` types (likely wrong fit — those are relative, not absolute).

Same encoding decision should generalize to future long/int/float/double/ip ranges, since `DATE_RANGE` is only the first of the range family to be modeled in ES|QL.

### 2. Add a coverage test.

A unit test in the Arrow module that iterates `DataType.values()` and asserts each type either (a) has a registered `BlockConverter` or (b) is in an explicit `ARROW_UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` deny-list with a comment explaining why. A PR that adds a new `DataType` without doing one or the other fails CI, forcing a conscious decision.

Sketch:

```java
public void testAllDataTypesCoveredByArrow() {
    Set<DataType> intentionallyUnsupported = Set.of(
        DataType.DOC_DATA_TYPE,    // internal plan type, never reaches output
        DataType.PARTIAL_AGG,      // internal aggregator state
        // ...add with a comment per entry
    );
    for (DataType t : DataType.values()) {
        if (intentionallyUnsupported.contains(t)) continue;
        assertNotNull(
            "DataType [" + t + "] has no Arrow converter. Either add one in "
            + "ArrowResponse.ESQL_CONVERTERS, or add it to intentionallyUnsupported "
            + "with a comment explaining why.",
            ArrowResponse.ESQL_CONVERTERS.get(t.esType())
        );
    }
}
```

Similar "expected = actual ∪ explicit exclusions" patterns are used elsewhere in the codebase for function registry coverage and capability checks, so this isn't a new convention.

## Scope

- [ ] Add `date_range` Arrow converter (encoding decision TBD in thread)
- [ ] Add coverage test + `ARROW_UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` set in the Arrow module
- [ ] Document the pattern in a comment near `ESQL_CONVERTERS`
- [ ] Extend to range family (long_range, integer_range, float_range, double_range, ip_range) once those are modeled as `DataType`s

Description

 Overview
I am opening this issue to request a smoother, automated upgrade path for migrating massive, long-lived indices to Elasticsearch 9.x. Currently, users face heavy manual reindexing burdens due to legacy index creation versions (v7) and breaking mapping changes, without a transparent, cluster-managed way to handle the migration.

 The Problem
Currently, the Upgrade Assistant flags several conditions that force a complete manual reindex before allowing an upgrade from ES 8 to ES 9. In our environment, we are blocked by two specific requirements:
1. Legacy Indices: The index was originally created in ES 7.
2. Mapping Incompatibilities: The Upgrade Assistant reports "Field mappings with incompatible percolator type", with the only provided solution being to reindex.

While the current Upgrade Assistant and the _reindex API are sufficient for smaller datasets, they become a severe operational burden for massive, live indices. Running a manual reindex on terabyte-scale data to fix underlying mapping types or version bumps requires complex orchestration and alias switchovers. This often results in unacceptable system downtime or performance degradation for live production environments.

 Our Context & Scale
In our production environment, we have a long-lived index that currently holds over 2 billion documents and is approximately 380 GiB in size.

Because our system cannot tolerate downtime, manually reindexing this massive dataset just to satisfy the version compatibility and percolator mapping requirements for ES 9 is extremely painful and risky, which becomes a significant blocker for our upgrade.

 Proposed Solution
We would like to request that the team provide an automated, internal resolution for these reindex triggers in a late 8.19.x version. Ideally, the cluster could transparently rewrite underlying Lucene segments (for v7 indices) and safely migrate incompatible field mappings (like percolator types) to v8/v9 compatible formats in the background.

If a full internal reindex is strictly required by the engine to resolve these conflicts, we request a zero-downtime, fully cluster-managed reindex feature. Elasticsearch should handle the underlying destination index creation, data copying, mapping transformations, and alias routing seamlessly behind the scenes, rather than forcing the customer to orchestrate the _reindex process manually.

Background

PR 144937 introduced a live in-flight counter (clientConnections) to cap how many concurrent requests ARS probes to stat-less or warming-up nodes across searches. The per-search cap (via searchCounts) works correctly. The cross-search cap has a known race.

 The race

The routing decision in rankNodes reads globalCounts (an unmodifiable view of clientConnections) to check whether the probe cap is reached. clientConnections is incremented later — inside the ConnectionCountingHandler constructor, at transport dispatch time. Between routing and dispatch, concurrent searches all read the same count (e.g. 0), all pass the cap, and all route to the new node before any increment lands.

 Fix direction

Move the increment to happen immediately after the routing decision, before concurrent searches can interleave. The core challenge is the decrement: decConnectionCount() is only called from ConnectionCountingHandler.handleResponse / handleException, which are only reachable if the handler was constructed. If getConnection() throws between the routing-time increment and handler construction, the counter leaks — permanently locking the node out of probe traffic.

The fix must decrement in every intermediate failure path between routing and successful handler construction (at minimum the getConnection() catch block in AbstractSearchAsyncAction).

Making clientConnections mutable (rather than introducing a separate reservations map) is preferred to avoid an additional structure with overlapping semantics.

When a shard times out during a search (SearchTimeoutException), the coordinator retries the request on the next available replica copy of that shard. If partial results are not allowed (allow_partial_search_results=false), this retry happens transparently before the timeout is surfaced to the user.

The issue was initially raised by @javanna in 72349.

> "when a shard times out, and partial results are not allowed, that timeout error is sent back to the coord node which will retry on another copy. That feels like the wrong behaviour, in that it defeats the purpose of providing a search timeout."

A related fix (149506) stopped retrying BAD_REQUEST errors on replicas. SearchTimeoutException was intentionally left out of that fix.

When a shard fails with SearchTimeoutException, the coordinator should treat it as a terminal failure for that shard group and not attempt any replica. The timeout should be surfaced to the user immediately, consistent with the intent of the search.timeout parameter.

Description

Time series data streams (TSDS) index documents based on their @timestamp and not the ingestion time because their value depends on this @timestamp.

A user can configure lifecycle actions such as downsampling or searchable snapshots that convert indices to read-only. As a consequence, documents with @timestamps that fall within these indices will be rejected. Effectively, a TSDS has a write window within which it should be able to accept documents that fall within this window.

This is not fully supported yet, because new TSDS cannot only go back till index.look_back_time, we are working on improving this, but before we do that we need a way to retrieve the write window of a TSDS regardless if the backing indices exist or not.

Implementation notes:

To define the write-window we need to:

1. Determine which lifecycle feature is currently managing this data stream (ILM or data stream lifecycle).
2. Determine how does each feature influence the write window, for example, which read-only actions in ILM.
~3. Expose it via the DataStream or something more appropriate.~

Description

A continuous transform's sync.time.delay is a single steady-state watermark: every checkpoint's upper time bound is now - delay. The delay has to be conservative enough to tolerate ingest/refresh lag in the source, so it is typically tens of seconds (Kibana SLO transforms use 65s, for example).

That single value also governs the very first checkpoint(s). When a transform starts (or is reset) and there is already data present — or data that lands moments after start — that data is not picked up until it has aged past the full steady-state delay. For a single transform that is a one-time delay; for chained transforms it compounds.

 Concrete motivation: Kibana SLO summary latency

Kibana SLOs are two chained continuous transforms: a rollup transform writes SLI documents, and a summary transform reads those SLI documents. Both use delay: 65s. On SLO creation:

1. The summary transform's first checkpoint fires immediately, before the rollup has written any SLI data, so it is empty.
2. The SLI data then lands a few seconds later.
3. Because every subsequent checkpoint uses the steady-state 65s delay, the just-written SLI data is not summarized until it ages past the 65s watermark.

The observed result is that the first SLO summary document appears ~60–120s after the SLO is created, which shows up as a visible lag in the SLO UI right after creation.

 Proposed enhancement

Add an optional initial_delay to sync.time:

 

Semantics:

- initial_delay is the reduced delay applied while the transform is still in its initial catch-up phase — i.e. until it has processed its first document. Once the transform has processed data it reverts to the steady-state delay.
- Keying off "has processed data" rather than literally "checkpoint 1" matters for chained transforms: the source data often lands shortly after the downstream transform's first (empty) checkpoint, so a checkpoint-1-only rule would revert to the steady-state delay before any data was ever seen.
- Defaults to delay when omitted, so existing transforms are completely unchanged. Must be <= delay.

 Scope / expected impact

This bounds the first-data latency by the transform's frequency instead of by delay + frequency. For the Kibana SLO summary transform (frequency: 1m) a local end-to-end test showed the first summary document dropping from ~122s to ~62s with no orchestration changes — purely by setting initial_delay. Reaching seconds-level latency additionally requires the downstream transform to be triggered promptly after the upstream writes (e.g. _schedule_now or a shorter frequency); that is out of scope here.

 Notes

- Backwards compatible on the wire (guarded by a new transport version) and in the persisted config (initial_delay is only serialized to XContent when it differs from delay).
- A PR implementing this will follow.

### Description

A continuous transform's `sync.time.delay` is a single steady-state watermark: every checkpoint's upper time bound is `now - delay`. The delay has to be conservative enough to tolerate ingest/refresh lag in the source, so it is typically tens of seconds (Kibana SLO transforms use `65s`, for example).

That single value also governs the **very first** checkpoint(s). When a transform starts (or is reset) and there is already data present — or data that lands moments after start — that data is not picked up until it has aged past the full steady-state `delay`. For a single transform that is a one-time delay; for **chained** transforms it compounds.

#### Concrete motivation: Kibana SLO summary latency

Kibana SLOs are two chained continuous transforms: a *rollup* transform writes SLI documents, and a *summary* transform reads those SLI documents. Both use `delay: 65s`. On SLO creation:

1. The summary transform's first checkpoint fires immediately, before the rollup has written any SLI data, so it is empty.
2. The SLI data then lands a few seconds later.
3. Because every subsequent checkpoint uses the steady-state `65s` delay, the just-written SLI data is not summarized until it ages past the `65s` watermark.

The observed result is that the **first SLO summary document appears ~60–120s after the SLO is created**, which shows up as a visible lag in the SLO UI right after creation.

### Proposed enhancement

Add an optional `initial_delay` to `sync.time`:

```json
"sync": {
  "time": {
    "field": "event.ingested",
    "delay": "65s",
    "initial_delay": "1s"
  }
}
```

Semantics:

- `initial_delay` is the reduced delay applied while the transform is still in its **initial catch-up phase** — i.e. until it has processed its first document. Once the transform has processed data it reverts to the steady-state `delay`.
- Keying off "has processed data" rather than literally "checkpoint #1" matters for chained transforms: the source data often lands shortly *after* the downstream transform's first (empty) checkpoint, so a checkpoint-#1-only rule would revert to the steady-state delay before any data was ever seen.
- Defaults to `delay` when omitted, so existing transforms are completely unchanged. Must be `<= delay`.

### Scope / expected impact

This bounds the first-data latency by the transform's `frequency` instead of by `delay + frequency`. For the Kibana SLO summary transform (`frequency: 1m`) a local end-to-end test showed the first summary document dropping from **~122s to ~62s** with no orchestration changes — purely by setting `initial_delay`. Reaching seconds-level latency additionally requires the downstream transform to be *triggered* promptly after the upstream writes (e.g. `_schedule_now` or a shorter `frequency`); that is out of scope here.

### Notes

- Backwards compatible on the wire (guarded by a new transport version) and in the persisted config (`initial_delay` is only serialized to XContent when it differs from `delay`).
- A PR implementing this will follow.

Data stream lifecycle (DLM) operates on the whole data stream. This means that if a user has a data stream that holds data for the last 6 months and adds any operations that needs to be executed after 7 days, then this operation will be applied to all the eligible indices older than 7 days at the next run.

If this operation is deleting 5+ months worth of data is not a problem, but if this operation is downsampling, this can have side-effects, downsampling is heavier and could overwhelm the master with persistent task updates. If the cluster is scaled properly it will eventually recover.

For this reasons, we want to add a flood gate mechanism so the lifecycle of a single data stream will not overload the cluster.

- [x] Expose actively downsampled indices ( 
- [ ] Add downsampling flood gate ( 

Note: this is issue is less probable with ILM because when a policy is changed on the data stream level it will affect new indices, unless specifically applied to all backing indices.

Observe that the GCP Region field is required — it cannot be left blank or set to global.

The GCP Region field should either:

Summary

RFC 10008: The HTTP QUERY Method became a Standards-Track RFC in June 2026, and it's essentially the spec written around what Elasticsearch search actually is: a request that's safe, idempotent, and cacheable, yet carries a body.

I'd like to propose supporting QUERY /{index}/_search as a first-class HTTP method, on equal footing with GET and POST. The server-side implementation is straightforward and completely additive. And here's the great news: Netty, the HTTP library Elasticsearch already uses, already recognizes QUERY as HttpMethod.QUERY. 

The only piece missing is adding QUERY to Elasticsearch's internal RestRequest.Method enum. It's a small change with outsized impact.

 QUERY is here now: the ecosystem is already ready

QUERY just became a registered HTTP method (June 2026), and support is rolling out across the stack. Here's what's already in place that matters for Elasticsearch:

- Netty (Elasticsearch's transport layer): QUERY is a full HttpMethod constant (HttpMethod.java line 92, described as “requests that the request target process the enclosed content in a safe and idempotent manner”). QUERY requests already traverse Elasticsearch's wire layer without issues.

- Apache HttpComponents Core (the go-to Java HTTP client): QUERY is marked as safe and idempotent (Method.java line 106). This is important because it influences the broader Java ecosystem.

- JDK java.net.http (Java's built-in): Developers can write HttpRequest.Builder.method(“QUERY”, …) and it just works (line 367). Only CONNECT is restricted.

- nginx, Node undici, axios: All have QUERY support merged or in flight. (nginx PR, undici PR 5459)

- OpenAPI 3.2: Officially added a query operation (OAI/OpenAPI-Specification 3033), so the Elasticsearch REST spec can describe QUERY endpoints.

- The adoption hub: Central coordination at jeswr/http-query-adoption.

Bottom line: clients can already send QUERY, proxies can already route it, and specifications can already describe it. Elasticsearch adding support completes the picture and makes ES a reference implementation in the ecosystem.

 Why this matters for Elasticsearch and REST

A search is fundamentally a read operation. But today, we're forced to express it in one of two ways that misrepresent what's actually happening:

1. POST /_search with a body: This works, but POST sends a signal to every client, proxy, and cache: “this request might mutate state.” That's wrong. Searches aren't safe, aren't idempotent, and aren't cacheable in the HTTP sense. We lose the ability to safely retry on timeout and we forfeit HTTP-level caching.

2. GET /_search with a body: This is closer to the intent, but a body on GET is not well-defined in the HTTP spec and many proxies, CDNs, and client libraries silently drop or reject it.

QUERY fills exactly this gap. It says plainly what a search is: a safe, idempotent, cacheable operation whose input is a body. Adding QUERY support makes Elasticsearch's REST API genuinely RESTful. The HTTP method finally carries the correct semantics. Intermediate caches can cache identical searches by content. Clients get safe-retry behavior without extra logic. It's a small change that elevates the entire search API.

 Current behavior

QUERY /{index}/_search returns 405 Method Not Allowed: not because the HTTP transport layer can't handle it, but because Elasticsearch's application-level method enum is closed:

- RestRequest.java L240-249: The enum reads Method { GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD, PATCH, TRACE, CONNECT } with no QUERY entry.
- When an unrecognized method arrives, RestController catches the IllegalArgumentException and routes it to handleUnsupportedHttpMethod(...), which returns METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED.

 
 curl: The problem today and the goal 

 
 

 Proposed change: three layers, additive and search-only

The RFC is more than “add a verb.” To do it right and get the full HTTP benefit, three surfaces are involved: the first is required for QUERY to work, and the other two unlock the semantic payoff:

1. The method (required). Add QUERY to RestRequest.Method and register it on the read routes (_search, and in follow-ups, _msearch and _count). Body parsing is identical to POST /_search. No handler code changes needed.

2. Body and Content-Type (RFC 10008 §2). QUERY defines its query by the Content-Type header of the request. For Elasticsearch, that's the existing application/json Query DSL. An empty body defaults to match-all (same as today). If Elasticsearch can't parse the Content-Type, return 415 Unsupported Media Type. If the Query DSL is malformed, return 400 (matching current _search behavior).

3. Cacheability and the Accept-Query header (RFC 10008 §2–§3). QUERY responses are cacheable with a cache key derived from request content (method + URI + body hash). Optionally advertise Accept-Query: application/json on the _search endpoint so proxies and CDNs know the endpoint accepts QUERY and understand the caching contract. Let responses carry appropriate Cache-Control headers. (The in-node request cache is unaffected. This is about HTTP-level caching at fronting proxies and CDNs, which matters a lot for read-heavy search traffic.)

Strictly read-only: no mutating route changes. GET and POST _search behavior is completely untouched.

 
 The change, concretely: illustrative diffs against main 

1) Add the method to server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/RestRequest.java
 

2) Register it on the search routes in server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/action/search/RestSearchAction.java (routes() method, around L94-99)
 
Because the handler already reads the body the same way for both GET and POST, no changes to prepareRequest(...) are needed for basic support to work. Add RestControllerTests + RestSearchAction unit tests, then a rest-api-spec YAML test for QUERY /_search.
 

 
 End-to-end: Java client using JDK HttpClient 

 
On the wire, Netty (transport-netty4) decodes the request line into HttpMethod.QUERY (already defined). The request hits RestController, which once QUERY is in RestRequest.Method and registered on RestSearchAction, dispatches to the same search handler as POST. It parses the same Query DSL body and returns the same hits. The only behavioral change is correct HTTP semantics: the method now correctly signals safe, idempotent, and cacheable intent.
 

 Backward compatibility
100% additive. Existing GET and POST _search clients are completely unaffected. QUERY is a newly accepted method on the same routes. No response shape or DSL changes, so this is purely opt-in for new clients.

 Questions for the team

Server implementation:
- Would you be interested in a PR adding QUERY support to _search (with follow-ups for _msearch and _count)?
- Should QUERY be gated behind a feature flag or RestApiVersion while clients and proxies catch up, or should we enable it directly?
- For the first PR, how much of the cacheability contract (Accept-Query and Cache-Control headers) should we include versus making that a follow-up?

Integration and ecosystem:
- The elasticsearch-java and opensearch-java client libraries will need to add QUERY to their HttpMethod enums before integration tests can fully exercise QUERY routes. Should the server PR wait for those, or should we move in parallel and coordinate the integration tests afterward?
- Should we provide migration guidance for users moving from POST/GET searches to QUERY? What should the adoption story look like?
- For higher-level HTTP client libraries (elasticsearch-py, elasticsearch-js, elasticsearch-go, elasticsearch-rs), what does the QUERY API look like from the user's perspective? Are there teams we should loop in early?

Rollout strategy:
- How do we coordinate timing with related projects (Java clients, official client libraries, proxies) to make the rollout smooth?

 References
- RFC 10008: The HTTP QUERY Method: 
- Netty HttpMethod.QUERY: 
- Apache HttpComponents Core Method.QUERY: 
- JDK java.net.http HttpRequest.Builder.method: 
- Node undici (RFC 10008): · nginx: 
- OpenAPI 3.2 query operation: 
- Adoption hub: 

Cross-platform coordination:
- A parallel feature request for OpenSearch has been filed at Synchronized rollout across both communities would help the ecosystem understand QUERY as a standard, not a one-off. 

I'm happy to implement this end-to-end: the RestController routing test, RestSearchAction unit test, and rest-api-spec YAML test, all under the DCO.

### Description

This is a fairly simple idea:

There are times when a specific shard of a larger index (or all of them) are lost. For example, if you have a readonly index and you ever remove your replica(s), then lose the primary shard(s) on a specific node, it may not be a serious concern other than the need to perform a partial restore.

In this scenario, when the cluster knows that it lost shards (the index is red), we should be able to perform a snapshot-restore without closing the index first.

The current approach requires:

```http
POST /.ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago/_close

POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/my-snapshot/_restore
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

I am proposing that this be simplified:

```http
POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/my-snapshot/_restore?missing_shards_only
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

I don't care about the added field name or whether it's a querystring parameter or body parameter, but something to a signify that this is okay and expected to be partial. This would seemingly help most red-index scenarios where a snapshot is available.

_Even better_ would be if we could do something where we don't even need to lookup the snapshot:

```http
POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/_restore?missing_shards_only
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

with the implication being that it comes from the latest successful snapshot for the index, per index if multiple are passed.

Problem

PR 153462 adds on_failure=ignore for columnar mode. When a field constraint fires and the violating value is redirected to the ._on_failure failure column, parseObjectOrField may also pre-capture the same value to _ignored_source via addIgnoredFieldFromContext before calling fieldMapper.parse(), for fields with fallback synthetic source mode or with sourceKeepMode == ARRAYS.

One confirmed instance: a field in FALLBACK synthetic source mode (e.g. keyword with a normalizer) that also has multi_value=false and on_failure=ignore will pre-capture the violated value into _ignored_source and also write it to ._on_failure, wasting disk since only one copy is emitted in the output. The same double-storage risk applies to ignore_malformed and any future fallback mechanism. The existing tests cover whether the feature fires (failure column is populated, _ignored is marked) but not whether it stores correctly. No test parameterizes over synthetic and columnar_stored source modes. No test asserts that _ignored_source is not simultaneously written for the same field and value, or that the violated value is absent from the main field doc values. No test verifies that GET _source returns identical results across source modes.

 Goal

Storage uniqueness tests (MapperServiceTestCase, parameterized over synthetic and columnar_stored). For each source mode and each violation type (multi_value=false and nullability=false), parse a document that triggers on_failure=ignore and inspect parsedDoc.rootDoc() directly: the main field doc values contain exactly the valid value; the ._on_failure sidecar field is present; _ignored_source does not also contain the violated value; _ignored is populated.

Semantic equivalence tests. SyntheticVersusColumnarStoredSourceIT already verifies equivalence between synthetic and columnar_stored for the general case but buildSpec() does not set multi_value=false, nullability=false, or on_failure=ignore. Extend the generator to exercise violation scenarios and assert that GET _source returns an identical document from both indices and that _ignored contains the field name in both cases. These tests also provide the safety net for the routing abstraction refactoring described in 153765, and will extend naturally to cover the ._on_failure read path once synthetic source reconstruction is wired.

Several binary doc-values queries construct their doc-values readers inside WeightscorerSupplier rather than in ScorerSupplierget:

- BinaryDvConfirmedQueryscorerSupplier builds the SortedBinaryDocValues used for wildcard confirmation before returning the supplier: 
- BinaryDocValuesContainsTermQueryscorerSupplier calls getBinaryDocValues and builds the two-phase iterator eagerly: 
- ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQueryscorerSupplier: 
- BinaryDocValuesLengthQueryscorerSupplier: 

On TSDB/logsdb segments, getBinaryDocValues constructs an AbstractTSDBDocValuesProducer$BinaryDecoder per query clause per segment: IndexInput clones, DirectMonotonicReader block tables, a per-block offsets array, and until 153903 also a decompression buffer sized to the largest uncompressed block in the segment (128k minimum).

This runs during query planning. BooleanScorerSupplier instantiates suppliers for every clause in order to compare costs before pulling any scorer, so for a query with many such clauses over many segments all of this state is allocated up front and held for the whole planning phase, including for clauses that never execute. Under high search concurrency this multiplies across threads; it contributed to the heap exhaustion investigated in where the failing allocation was inside BinaryDvConfirmedQuery$1.scorerSupplier while threads were still in BooleanScorerSupplier.computeCost. 153903 mitigates the largest single allocation by allocating the buffer lazily, but the reader construction itself is still eager in all four queries.

 Lucene contract

The ScorerSupplier API exists to separate cost estimation from scorer construction. From the Lucene 10.5 javadoc:

- ScorerSupplier: "A supplier of Scorer. This allows to get an estimate of the cost before building the Scorer."
- ScorerSupplierget(long leadCost): "Get the Scorer. This may not return null and must be called at most once."
- WeightscorerSupplier(LeafReaderContext): "Get a ScorerSupplier, which allows knowing the cost of the Scorer before building it. A scorer supplier for the same LeafReaderContext instance may be requested multiple times as part of a single search call."

Since get is called at most once and only for clauses that actually execute, expensive per-leaf setup belongs there; work done in scorerSupplier is paid for every clause during planning and may even be paid multiple times per leaf. IndexOrDocValuesQuery is the canonical consumer of this split: it requests both suppliers, compares costs, and discards one without ever calling get on it.

There is precedent for this kind of deferral in BinaryDvConfirmedQuery: 136086 delayed automaton creation for the same reason (OOM on queries against wildcard fields).

Relates to 153903.

Context (Threshold)

Threshold rules support an optional cardinality condition: a group alerts only if the number of distinct values of a chosen field meets a configured value (e.g. "≥ 10 distinct user.name"). In ES|QL we express this with COUNT_DISTINCT( ) BY .

 What we're seeing

The Threshold ES|QL query works and passes tests in general, but with the cardinality condition it fails with performance errors on high-cardinality data, and COUNT_DISTINCT carries a documented accuracy limit around 40,000 distinct values.

Two distinct concerns for this rule type:
- Failures at high cardinality make otherwise-valid cardinality-threshold rules unrunnable on realistic data.
- Approximate counts are boundary-sensitive here. Unlike a dashboard where a ~1% error is cosmetic, a Threshold rule compares the distinct count directly against the configured value — so an approximate count near the threshold can flip an alert on or off (false positives/negatives) rather than just being slightly off.

 How this maps to current rule behavior

The current (_search-based) implementation uses a cardinality aggregation for this condition; the migration relies on COUNT_DISTINCT as the equivalent.

Summary

CSV and TSV files from government and vendor exports often start with a few non-data lines (generation timestamp, legal disclaimer) and only then the real header row. Federation today treats the first line as the header when header_row is true, so those files parse as garbage or fail.

Request: Databricks-style behavior — skip a fixed number of leading rows, then treat the next remaining row as the header.

This is table stakes vs Databricks, Athena/Hive, BigQuery, and DuckDB. Snowflake has SKIP_HEADER, but it cannot be combined with PARSE_HEADER. Databricks is the model we want: skipRows and header=true work together.

 Current behavior

Dataset CSV/TSV settings today (docs):

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| header_row | true | First row names the columns |
| comment | // | Skip lines that begin with this prefix |
| error_mode | fail_fast | Malformed-row handling |

There is no count of leading rows to ignore. A prose disclaimer is not a // comment, so comment does not help. With header_row: true, line 1 becomes the column names.

 Requested behavior (Databricks)

From the Databricks Spark CSV options:

> skipRows — The number of rows from the beginning of the CSV file that should be ignored, including commented and empty rows. If header is true, the header will be the first unskipped and uncommented row.

Proposed dataset setting, e.g. skip_rows (integer, default 0), combined with existing header_row and comment:

1. Ignore the first skip_rows lines of the file (including blank and comment-prefixed lines in that count).
2. If header_row is true, the next remaining non-comment line is the header.
3. Remaining lines are data rows.

Example file:

 

 

Expected columns: state, ip, user_agent. Expected first data row: TX, 1.2.3.4, Mozilla/5.0.

Today this dataset either fails or invents columns from File generated 2026-09-11.

 What we are not asking for

- Auto-detecting which line is the header (DuckDB sniff_csv / unknown-length preambles). Athena documents that variable-length headers are out of scope. Field users who hit this already know N.
- Parquet / Iceberg / NDJSON. Schema lives in file metadata or every line is a record. This is a delimited-text problem.

 Impact

Field testing of Experimental federation hit this on public government CSV in S3. The workaround is to copy the object and hand-delete the preamble, which defeats query-in-place.

Same pattern shows up in agency extracts, vendor reports, and Excel-exported CSVs. Without skip_rows, those objects are not queryable as datasets even when the data rows themselves are well-formed.

 Suggestions

1. Add skip_rows (non-negative integer, default 0) on CSV/TSV dataset settings.
2. Apply it before header_row resolution, matching Databricks: skip N, then first remaining uncommented row is the header when header_row is true.
3. Document interaction with comment (does skip_rows count comment lines, as Databricks does?).
4. Out of scope for this issue: sniffer / “find the column labels.”

## Current behavior

Dataset CSV/TSV settings today ([docs](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/esql-data-federation-datasets)):

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `header_row` | `true` | First row names the columns |
| `comment` | `//` | Skip lines that begin with this prefix |
| `error_mode` | `fail_fast` | Malformed-row handling |

## Requested behavior (Databricks)

From the [Databricks Spark CSV options](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/spark/api-options):

1. Ignore the first `skip_rows` lines of the file (including blank and comment-prefixed lines in that count).
2. If `header_row` is `true`, the next remaining non-comment line is the header.
3. Remaining lines are data rows.

Example file:

```
File generated 2026-09-11
CONFIDENTIAL — authorized use only
state,ip,user_agent
TX,1.2.3.4,Mozilla/5.0
```

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "format": "csv",
    "skip_rows": 2,
    "header_row": true
  }
}
```

Expected columns: `state`, `ip`, `user_agent`. Expected first data row: `TX`, `1.2.3.4`, `Mozilla/5.0`.

Today this dataset either fails or invents columns from `File generated 2026-09-11`.

- Auto-detecting which line is the header (DuckDB `sniff_csv` / unknown-length preambles). Athena documents that variable-length headers are out of scope. Field users who hit this already know N.
- Parquet / Iceberg / NDJSON. Schema lives in file metadata or every line is a record. This is a delimited-text problem.

## Impact

Field testing of Experimental federation hit this on public government CSV in S3. The workaround is to copy the object and hand-delete the preamble, which defeats query-in-place.

Same pattern shows up in agency extracts, vendor reports, and Excel-exported CSVs. Without `skip_rows`, those objects are not queryable as datasets even when the data rows themselves are well-formed.

## Suggestions

1. Add `skip_rows` (non-negative integer, default `0`) on CSV/TSV dataset settings.
2. Apply it before `header_row` resolution, matching Databricks: skip N, then first remaining uncommented row is the header when `header_row` is true.
3. Document interaction with `comment` (does `skip_rows` count comment lines, as Databricks does?).

When a relocated PIT's BCC is already uploaded, TransportStatelessUnpromotableRelocationActionfetchOpenPitContextInfo reads the compound commit from the object store and overrideBlobFileRangesTimestamp rewrites generational files to that commit's locations. The target opens them from one BCC.

When the BCC is not uploaded, the handoff uses SearchDirectory metadata. Generational files stay on the first BCC that contained them, so one PIT commit can reference several BCCs (even though the PIT BCC should have all necessary copies of generational files). 

The search node does not have the unuploaded virtual BCC's StatelessCompoundCommits, so it cannot call overrideBlobFileRangesTimestamp on that path. Either of these would provide them:

- Read the unuploaded virtual BCC from the indexing node (readVirtualBatchedCompoundCommitChunk).
- Keep the virtual BCC's unuploaded StatelessCompoundCommits on the search node.

The handoff could then send the latest generational-file locations, matching the uploaded path.

## Problem

When an ES|QL rule batch (analyzer or optimizer) fails to converge, the query fails with:

```
Rule execution limit [100] reached
```

The message does not say which rules kept changing the plan, so every occurrence needs a local reproduction with `TRACE` logging on the `.changes` loggers before anyone can tell where the loop is. In serverless this is often impossible, because the failing query depends on cross-project state that cannot be reproduced locally.

Example: the analyzer loop fixed in #160159. The query

```
SET unmapped_fields="load";
FROM (FROM sample_data), (FROM sample_data)
| WHERE TO_STRING(client_ip) == "172.21.3.15" OR does_not_exist IS NOT NULL
| EVAL ip = TO_STRING(client_ip)
| LIMIT 5
```

only reported `Rule execution limit [100] reached`, and finding that `ResolveUnionTypesInUnionAll` was the rule re-adding a column on every pass took a manual investigation.

## Proposal

Keep the names of the last 10 rules that changed the plan in the batch that hit the limit, and add them to the message:

```
Rule execution limit [100] reached. Last Rules: [analysis.Analyzer$ResolveUnionTypesInUnionAll, analysis.Analyzer$ResolveUnionTypesInUnionAll, ...]
```

Rules that ran without changing the plan are left out, since they cannot be what keeps the batch from converging.
kept_issues.title: ES|QL: Rule execution limit error does not name the looping rules
